segments.title: Why Britain preferred an independent Hawaii
segments.body: Britain valued Hawaii chiefly as a neutral port where warships and merchants could obtain water and supplies. American interests were more closely tied to trans-Pacific trade, while Britain's principal imperial routes ran through other oceans. Annexation would add a commitment to defend islands that offered Britain little additional advantage. Hawaiian rulers tried to preserve independence by balancing foreign interests, including through appointments to their council. That balance became harder to maintain when merchants faced exclusion or alleged religious prejudice in legal proceedings. Consular and ministerial ties then turned private disputes into an international confrontation.

evidence.note: British access to an open neutral port, American trans-Pacific interests, Hawaiian balancing policy, and the grievances that threatened it.

segments.summary: Britain valued Hawaii as an open, neutral stopping place for warships and merchants but saw little advantage in acquiring and defending the islands.

segments.title: Evacuating a fort without saving its guns
segments.body: The later French landing illustrates the limits of Hawaii's military preparations. Most defenders had left the fort, but its guns remained available for the French to spike. If there was time to plan an evacuation, removing the weapons offered another possible precaution. Preserved guns might have supported an attempt to retake the fort later; their loss reduced that option.

evidence.note: An evacuation before the French landing left guns to be spiked, with their removal proposed as a possible aid to recapture.

segments.summary: The criticism of Hawaii's fort evacuation concerns the guns left behind and the possibility of preserving them for a later counterattack.

segments.title: Overseas experience and the loss of Hawaiian ministers
segments.body: Hawaii combined an advanced, organized state with inadequate preparation for the demands of foreign relations. Ministers who visited Britain and America could have helped the kingdom understand other powers and preserve its independence later in the nineteenth century. Repeated reports of their deaths in storms prompt suspicion, although severe weather remains an explicit possible explanation. The causes remain unresolved, but the losses removed ministers who might have helped prepare Hawaii for foreign pressure.

evidence.note: Hawaiian state capacity, ministers' overseas visits, reported storm deaths, and the explicit possibility of natural weather causes.

segments.summary: The loss of ministers with overseas experience raises questions about Hawaii's preparations and the uncertain circumstances of reported deaths in storms.

segments.title: Unpaid merchant consuls and missionary influence in Hawaii
segments.body: Richard Charlton's consular appointment combined diplomatic duties with private commercial interests. After the Hawaiian royal visitors died in London in 1824, Britain sought more formal relations with the islands and followed the American practice of appointing an unpaid merchant representative. Charlton reached Hawaii in 1825 after earlier experience in the Pacific. Hiram Bingham's conservative Congregationalist outlook brought religious influence into disputes over commerce and social conduct. A Hawaiian minister interested in developing the economy also clashed with missionaries over behaviour they opposed. Combining mercantile business, consular office and religious influence created repeated opportunities for a private dispute to acquire official backing.

evidence.note: Charlton's Pacific background, appointment and arrival, Bingham's religious outlook, and early conflicts over commerce and conduct.

segments.summary: Charlton combined trade with an unpaid consular post, while Hiram Bingham and fellow missionaries influenced Hawaiian government and social policy.

segments.title: A disputed marriage payment became a libel dispute
segments.body: Missionary William Richards accused Captain William Buckle of trafficking a woman after a payment connected with their marriage. The payment was more likely a dowry for a marriage outside the missionaries' church. Richards may nevertheless have understood the payment as trafficking within his own religious assumptions. An attempt to send him to England for libel proceedings collided with the queen's declaration of his innocence after Bingham supported him. The disagreement combined competing interpretations of marriage with religious influence over the proposed legal remedy.

evidence.note: The trafficking allegation, the proposed dowry explanation, Richards' possible understanding, and royal intervention in the proposed libel proceedings.

segments.summary: The Buckle-Richards dispute joined incompatible views of a marriage payment to a failed attempt at libel proceedings.

segments.title: HMS Sulphur brought Catholic priests to prevent a wider dispute
segments.body: Charlton sought naval help to free two British prisoners believed to have been detained for religious reasons. HMS Sulphur brought Catholic priests to Hawaii in 1837 to open a parish. Catholic sailors and other residents gave the Royal Navy a reason to support access to worship. The diplomatic concern was that France or Spain might otherwise deliver the priests themselves. Expelling clergy landed by either Catholic power could then become a pretext for war. British delivery of the priests was intended to reduce that danger while supporting religious balance.

evidence.note: A request for naval help over alleged religious detention, the 1837 delivery of Catholic priests by HMS Sulphur, and concern that their expulsion after a French or Spanish landing could become a casus belli.

segments.summary: The Royal Navy's support for Catholic worship also sought to avoid a confrontation over clergy brought by France or Spain.

segments.title: Merchant rivalry trapped the Royal Navy in a national dispute
segments.body: Charlton left Hawaii in September 1842 to present his complaints to the British government. On the way he encountered Captain Lord George Paulet of HMS Carysfort and alleged that proceedings were being rigged against him. Juries composed largely of American merchants later ruled against Charlton in his absence, although the merits of his opponents' cases remain open to argument. Rear Admiral Richard Darton Thomas authorized Paulet to investigate and report. Charlton's consular office made the dispute appear to Paulet as an affront to the British Crown. The criticism of Judd concerns his handling of this feud, despite his otherwise capable administration: personal rivalry and ministerial authority became entangled. He was a Hawaiian minister, while the American representative was his trading partner. Those overlapping connections made a commercial quarrel increasingly difficult to contain.

evidence.note: Charlton's departure and allegations, disputed legal merits, Thomas's investigative instructions, and the official and commercial roles behind the confrontation.

segments.summary: Charlton's disputed claims acquired national importance through his consular office, while Judd's commercial connections complicated his Hawaiian ministerial role.

segments.title: Rejecting the acting consul removed the diplomatic safety valve
segments.body: When Paulet arrived, Kamehameha III was away from Honolulu and Charlton's appointed replacement, Alexander Simpson, was not recognized as acting consul. Rejecting Simpson allowed Charlton's opponents to proceed without his appointed representative in court. It also removed the official who could explain local delays and carry messages between the government and the visiting warship. Paulet was not a Pacific specialist and relied on formal procedure. The refusal therefore left the Hawaiian government communicating directly with a naval captain who had less diplomatic flexibility than a consul.

evidence.note: The king's absence, expectations of naval access to a ruler, and the loss of the acting consul as an intermediary.

segments.summary: Hawaii's refusal to recognize Charlton's deputy left HMS Carysfort communicating directly with the government and deprived both sides of a consular intermediary.

segments.title: A refused private interview hardened Paulet's position
segments.body: Paulet's letter of 11 February requested immediate information about when the king could return, with a voyage to the king's residence as the alternative. The governor replied that he would find a vessel to summon the king from Maui, allowing about six days if the wind permitted. On 16 February Paulet requested a private interview for the following day, accompanied by a competent interpreter. Kamehameha III declined and offered Judd as his confidential agent. Since Paulet regarded Judd as the prime mover behind the alleged injuries to British subjects, the reply made compromise harder. Paulet refused to deal with Judd and demanded compliance with his enclosed terms by 4 p.m. the next day, threatening coercive action if they were rejected.

evidence.note: The February letters, the governor's estimated return time, the refused interview, Judd's proposed role, and Paulet's deadline for compliance.

segments.summary: Paulet requested a direct meeting with Kamehameha III, but the king referred him to Judd - the official at the center of the British complaints.

segments.title: Paulet's demands focused on consular standing and legal treatment
segments.body: Paulet's first demand sought removal of the attachment on Charlton's property, restoration of land taken by the government, and reparation for the losses. The second required recognition of Simpson as acting consul, accompanied by a public reception of his commission and a British flag salute that Carysfort would return. British subjects were not to be imprisoned in fetters unless accused of an offense considered a felony under English law. A promised fair retrial in Henry Skinner's case against an American citizen was also required. The remaining demands called for juries with a British half approved by the consul, jurors free of personal interest or prejudgment, and direct communication between the acting consul and the king. The mixed-jury provision belonged to an existing framework for resolving disputes across different legal systems. These demands sought legal and diplomatic redress without calling for a transfer of sovereignty.

evidence.note: The six demands and the existing framework for mixed juries in disputes involving different legal systems.

segments.summary: The ultimatum demanded consular recognition, property redress, limits on fetters, a promised retrial, mixed juries, and direct access to the king.

segments.title: Separating Charlton's property dispute from his consular status
segments.body: Charlton's private landholdings could also be treated as consular grounds because he combined business with an official appointment. Even a judgment valid on its private merits could therefore appear to Britain as an attack on diplomatic standing. One proposed route out was to recognize Simpson as acting consul and seek British agreement to replace Charlton before pursuing the property claim. That sequence would have separated the dispute over land from the question of who represented the British government.

evidence.note: Possible consular status of Charlton's land and the proposed sequence of recognizing Simpson, replacing Charlton, and pursuing property claims.

segments.summary: Recognizing Simpson and formally replacing Charlton offered a possible way to pursue private land claims without provoking a dispute over consular standing.

segments.title: USS Boston and the cost of intervening in Hawaii
segments.body: USS Boston remained in the harbour as the dispute escalated. Accounts differ over whether people urged her captain to intervene, but he did not start a confrontation with the British frigate. The argument against intervention centres on the danger of turning aggressive commercial rivalries into another war with Britain. Memories of the War of 1812, inadequate naval infrastructure and poor congressional funding form part of that assessment. Meanwhile, the Hawaiian king agreed to receive Paulet and the British representative on 20 February at 11 a.m.

evidence.note: Boston's presence, uncertain approaches urging intervention, the assessment of American naval readiness, and the king's agreement to meet on 20 February.

segments.summary: The case against USS Boston's intervention rested on naval readiness and the risk of another war with Britain, before the king agreed to a meeting.

segments.title: Failed negotiations led to a provisional cession
segments.body: The Hawaiian government recognized Simpson as acting consul, and daily meetings followed between 20 and 23 February. Kamehameha III agreed to reopen disputed cases but maintained that he would not overrule the courts or disregard due process. The competing land claims left room for argument on both sides, while the involvement of a Hawaiian minister and Britain's consul made their handling a diplomatic problem. On 25 February 1843, the king signed a conditional cession to Paulet. Its reservations protected any arrangement already reached by Hawaiian representatives abroad and otherwise placed the outcome before the British government after it received both sides' information. The cession left the ultimate settlement open while transferring authority under local pressure.

evidence.note: Recognition of Simpson, meetings over disputed judgments, arguable claims on both sides, and the reservations in the deed of cession.

segments.summary: After several meetings failed to reconcile legal process with British demands, Kamehameha III provisionally ceded the islands pending a decision by Queen Victoria's government.

segments.title: Paulet preserved Hawaiian administration under temporary control
segments.body: Paulet's proclamation kept the Hawaiian population under the administration of the king, chiefs, and their officers. The king or his deputy also sat on the commission alongside Paulet and two other members. That commission handled relations with foreign powers, except negotiations with Britain, and arrangements among foreign residents. Existing Hawaiian laws remained the basis of justice, while the king and chiefs could make further laws and communicate them to the commission. Revenue officers and government archives remained in Hawaiian hands, although the commission could inspect the accounts and government vessels could be required for British service. The proclamation barred land transactions by the commission and transfers from Hawaiian owners to foreigners pending Britain's decision. Existing bona fide obligations remained enforceable as though the cession had never occurred.

evidence.note: Division of authority, continued laws and revenue administration, inspection powers, government vessels, specified land restrictions, and existing obligations.

segments.summary: The king and chiefs retained domestic administration, while a commission supervised foreign affairs and restricted specified land transactions.

segments.title: Hawaiian and British envoys carried rival accounts abroad
segments.body: Paulet sent Simpson to Britain to explain events since Charlton's departure, while Judd chose the merchant James F. B. Marshall to present Hawaii's case abroad. Marshall left aboard the British ship Albert, although accounts differ over whether he declared only a business journey or whether his diplomatic purpose was understood. He carried his case to Boston and then London, approaching newspapers and contacts who could support Hawaiian representations. Lord Aberdeen had already stated on 1 April 1843 that Britain was willing and determined to recognize the Sandwich Islands' independence under their existing sovereign. Simpson reached Britain in late May or early June, and Marshall arrived on 30 June. Their accounts therefore arrived after that policy decision. The remaining task was to settle the grievances without humiliating either government.

evidence.note: Simpson's dispatch, uncertainty over Marshall's declared purpose, his route through Boston to London, and Aberdeen's policy preceding their arrival.

segments.summary: Simpson sailed for Britain while James F. B. Marshall sought American and Hawaiian diplomatic support, but London had already chosen to recognize Hawaiian independence.

segments.title: The U.S. Pacific Squadron watched without forcing a confrontation
segments.body: USS Constellation reached Hawaii in early July, followed on 22 July by USS United States carrying Commodore Thomas ap Catesby Jones. Jones consulted American representatives and observed events without moving to expel the British. As Pacific Squadron commander, he had to consider the forces a conflict would bring against him. HMS Carysfort and Thomas's approaching flagship, HMS Dublin, together made the local forces roughly balanced.

evidence.note: American ship arrivals, Jones's observation and consultations, and the comparison with Carysfort and the approaching Dublin.

segments.summary: USS Constellation and USS United States observed the provisional government without attempting to expel the British.

segments.title: The Hawaiian cession did not end Paulet's naval career
segments.body: The defence of Paulet's conduct rests on his duty to protect the British Crown's standing. Once he had accepted the cession, finding a way back became a task for a more senior officer. The affair nevertheless left him able to continue his Royal Navy career, including service in the Crimean War. He eventually became an admiral, so the diplomatic reversal in Hawaii did not end his advancement.

evidence.note: The interpretation of Paulet's duties, his continued naval career, and the need for another officer to resolve the cession.

segments.summary: Paulet continued to Crimean War service and eventual flag rank, while a superior officer had to resolve the diplomatic consequences in Hawaii.

segments.title: Admiral Thomas restored Kamehameha III's sovereignty
segments.body: Rear Admiral Richard Darton Thomas arrived on 26 July after dealing with other Pacific Station responsibilities around South America. He immediately requested a personal interview with Kamehameha III. His declaration examined whether the disputed demands made surrender unavoidable and whether the cession had been a free, unbiased, unsolicited act of sovereign authority. Having established that the difficulties could be overcome and obtained the king's assent to new proposals, Thomas formally declined the cession on 31 July. He recognized Kamehameha III as the legitimate independent sovereign and left the administration of justice in Hawaiian hands.

evidence.note: Thomas's arrival and interview, examination of the circumstances of cession, the king's acceptance of new proposals, and restoration of sovereign authority.

segments.summary: Rear Admiral Richard Thomas reached Honolulu, met the king, secured an acceptable settlement, and rejected the provisional cession on 31 July 1843.

segments.title: A station commander could combine naval and diplomatic power
segments.body: A frigate captain had fewer diplomatic options than a regional commander-in-chief. A captain normally depended on a consul to mediate, while Thomas could combine naval command with broader authority to negotiate. The king's acceptance of new proposals supplied the common ground for restoring sovereignty. The declaration required governments to protect foreign residents and avoid sanctioning injuries committed by their own subjects. Its accompanying interpretation applies that obligation to both Hawaiian ministers and British consular officials whose private disputes had become national affronts. Thomas combined the negotiated restoration with a warning that another unresolved grievance could bring the commander-in-chief and a larger force.

evidence.note: Thomas's wider authority, consular mediation, the new proposals, duties toward foreign residents, and the warning of further naval action.

segments.summary: Thomas had the authority to offer compromise while retaining a credible warning that repeated injustice could bring a much larger naval response.

segments.title: How to read nineteenth-century diplomatic boilerplate
segments.body: Thomas's declaration closes with claims about Captain Cook, George Vancouver, American missionaries, Christianity, commerce and civilization. These claims belong to the declaration's nineteenth-century diplomatic language. Much of the long letter uses conventional phrasing, while only a few sentences establish actions or obligations. Separating those operative provisions from the surrounding rhetoric makes the document easier to interpret. Its closing paragraphs return to justice and commerce before dating the declaration aboard HMS Dublin at Honolulu on 31 July 1843.

evidence.note: The declaration's closing historical and religious claims, conventional diplomatic language, few actionable sentences, and date aboard HMS Dublin.

segments.summary: Thomas's long declaration shows how a few operative promises and warnings could be embedded within conventional language about civilization, religion, commerce, and friendship.

segments.title: Thomas's naval career prepared him for Pacific diplomacy
segments.body: Richard Darton Thomas combined a long naval career with experience of diplomatic disputes. His service included wartime ship commands and responsibility for vessels in ordinary at Portsmouth and Plymouth. In the Pacific he had dealt with the French occupation of Tahiti and worked with American interests. Those dealings earned him a reputation as a capable intermediary. He arrived in Hawaii with experience of the sovereignty disputes that a frigate captain could find difficult to resolve.

evidence.note: Thomas's naval service, ships in ordinary, diplomatic work in South America and the Pacific, and dealings with American interests.

segments.summary: Experience around South America, the French occupation of Tahiti and dealings with American interests prepared Thomas to negotiate in Hawaii.

segments.title: Dublin's advantage depended on fighting range and an uncertain gun total
segments.body: HMS Dublin was a razeed third rate with heavy 32-pounder guns. At close range, an American ship's carronades could deliver a broadside strong enough to outmatch her. At medium and longer ranges, Dublin's guns and the experience of her crew are judged likely to give her an advantage. Her precise armament remains uncertain here: a 40-gun figure for 1840 is compared with another account giving 48 guns. Additional carronades and modifications made before Thomas took the ship out offer a possible explanation, but the competing figures remain unresolved. A description of Thomas as caring more for guns than silverware fits that proposed modification without proving it.

evidence.note: Conditional comparison with American carronades, Dublin's 32-pounders and razeed classification, competing 40- and 48-gun figures, and a possible modified armament.

segments.summary: HMS Dublin's 32-pounders favoured a fight at longer ranges, while American carronades and conflicting gun totals qualify a simple comparison of ship strength.

segments.title: Judd's role as intermediary and the escalation of the crisis
segments.body: A prompt personal meeting between Kamehameha III and Paulet might have prevented the affair from escalating. Directing Paulet to negotiate through Judd instead put the accused minister between the captain and the king. Paulet probably went too far, but his direct approach and reliance on force made him a poor fit for this crisis rather than simply a bad officer. Thomas succeeded partly because experience, rank, and broader powers allowed him to think laterally and reopen the encounter on different terms.

evidence.note: The possibility of an early royal interview, Judd's proposed intermediary role, Paulet's forceful approach and Thomas's broader experience.

segments.summary: Trying to make Judd the intermediary when he was the subject of complaint encouraged a direct, forceful officer to treat the crisis as a problem for coercion.

segments.title: Most-favored-nation treatment protected British residents
segments.body: Kamehameha III promised protection to British subjects living in his dominions. They would receive any rights, privileges and immunities already granted, or later granted, to the most favored foreign nation. Giving another country's residents better terms would therefore extend those terms to British residents too. Similar clauses in other powers' agreements could spread the same privileges across several foreign communities.

evidence.note: Article one and the explanation of most-favored-nation privileges.

segments.summary: The first article gave British subjects the best privileges Hawaii granted to any foreign nationality.

segments.title: Captains gained direct access to the king through interpreters
segments.body: A visiting British warship captain could request an interview after giving proper notice of its purpose. Each side could bring a competent interpreter, whose role was strictly limited to interpreting. Judd could therefore have attended as the king's interpreter, with Simpson interpreting for Paulet. That arrangement would have allowed the king to hear the captain's complaints directly. The distinction between translating and conducting negotiations addressed the earlier dispute over using Judd as an intermediary.

evidence.note: Article two's interview and interpreter provisions, including Judd and Simpson as an acceptable hypothetical arrangement.

segments.summary: The second article required interviews with visiting British captains and confined interpreters to translating.

segments.title: The agreement settled property claims and changed trial safeguards
segments.body: The agreement recorded the removal of the attachment on Charlton's property and the restoration of land that belonged to him. The suit had been brought while both plaintiff and defendant were absent, and the king promised that it would not be renewed under similar circumstances. British subjects were not to be confined in fetters unless they were riotous or quarrelsome, and then only for their security. The consul, or a British substitute he nominated, could attend proceedings. Where arbitration failed and local law had to decide a dispute, half the jury would consist of British subjects approved by the consul. Jurors had to swear that they had neither prejudged the case nor held an interest in its outcome.

evidence.note: Articles three to five on Charlton's property, restraints, consular attendance and jury composition.

segments.summary: Charlton's property, detention in fetters and British participation in juries received separate safeguards.

segments.title: Consular access came with a defined right to object
segments.body: Important complaints affecting British subjects were to reach the king and his council through the accredited consul or an authorized substitute. The purpose was to facilitate referral to the proper courts before the matter reached the British government. The king promised to recognize duly appointed consuls and give them access when British grievances required it. He retained the right to object to an acting consul who had violated Hawaiian law, defied royal authority, caused disturbances, or given other sufficient grounds for objection. Those reasons would be submitted to Britain. An acting consul who faced no such objection would receive the protection and freedom needed to perform the office.

evidence.note: Articles six and seven on direct communication, recognition, grounds for objection and protection of acting consuls.

segments.summary: The king accepted direct consular communication while retaining grounds to challenge an acting appointment.

segments.title: Unresolved claims went to London under a sovereignty safeguard
segments.body: British grievances outside the earlier articles were referred to the British government for a considered settlement. Hawaiian representation at the Court of St James was one route for that process. When the king and chiefs considered appeals affecting British residents' interests or property, the consul or a substitute could attend with an interpreter and offer advice. Britain retained the power to approve, ratify or modify the agreement, which also had to respect existing arrangements. The final article expressly preserved the inherent or acknowledged rights of an independent sovereign. Keeping ministers and diplomats from using their offices in private financial disputes was central to preventing another crisis.

evidence.note: Articles eight to ten on outstanding claims, consular advice on appeals, British ratification and sovereign rights, followed by the warning against mixing private disputes with office.

segments.summary: The final articles referred outstanding claims to Britain, admitted consular advice on appeals and preserved the king's rights as an independent sovereign.

segments.title: Britain rejected annexation and moved toward professional diplomats
segments.body: Neither the demands nor the settlement proposed permanent British rule, and Aberdeen had already committed the government to recognizing the existing Hawaiian sovereign. American and British naval officers socialized throughout the apparent confrontation, helping defuse any risk of a battle between their ships. Paulet accepted the limits he had set and yielded authority as soon as Thomas arrived. In the longer term, Britain increasingly moved away from relying on merchants who combined personal business with diplomatic office.

evidence.note: Aberdeen's independence policy, naval officers' social contacts, Paulet's transfer of authority and Britain's move toward regular diplomats.

segments.summary: British policy consistently favored Hawaiian independence, while the affair exposed the danger of giving private merchants consular authority.

segments.title: Restoration Day and Thomas Square commemorated the settlement
segments.body: The king promised that no subject would be punished for acts injuring his government between 25 February and the restoration. His proclamation also ordered the release of prisoners and suspended business for ten days of celebration. At the ceremony the British flag came down and the Hawaiian flag rose, accompanied by 21-gun salutes from the fort, park guns and HMS Carysfort, Dublin and Hazard. Honolulu's Thomas Square was named for the admiral and commemorates the place of restoration. At the time of the recording, it was described as one of four places in Hawaii where the Hawaiian flag could fly without the United States flag.

evidence.note: The amnesty, release of prisoners, ten-day celebration, flag ceremony, named ships' salutes and Thomas Square's commemorative role.

segments.summary: Kamehameha III proclaimed amnesty and celebration, while the flag ceremony and Thomas Square preserved the memory of Admiral Thomas's restoration of Hawaiian rule.

segments.title: The French occupation of 1849 followed a harsher pattern
segments.body: France had agreed in 1843 to avoid taking possession of Hawaiian territory. Its consul was later told to avoid a belligerent manner, yet believed that displaying a French corvette could force concessions. The complaints concerned Catholic worship and French trade, with religious restrictions also serving to obstruct commercial activity. One demand sought compensation from Hawaii for damage to a French hotelkeeper's property attributed to British sailors. In 1849 about 140 French Marines, supported by sailors and two field pieces, landed and occupied an almost empty fort. They spiked or destroyed the coastal guns, caused roughly $100,000 in damage, and took the king's yacht to Tahiti without returning it. The occupation lasted from late August to 5 September.

evidence.note: France's earlier commitment, consular pressure, religious and trade grievances, the hotelkeeper's claim, and the 1849 landing, destruction and seizure of the yacht.

segments.summary: French forces pressed religious and commercial complaints, then occupied a fort, destroyed guns and property, and took the king's yacht.

segments.title: Judd sought outside support but France refused reparations
segments.body: Judd travelled to settle the incident and sought support from Britain and the United States. British naval officers involved in the Paulet Affair helped him obtain support despite their earlier objections to his conduct in office. The French government initially condemned the attack on Honolulu. After receiving its officers' accounts, it decided that the action had been justified and refused reparations. Britain and the United States declined to take the dispute further on Hawaii's behalf. The contrast with 1843 centres on a French seizure led by an admiral and the failure to obtain compensation afterward.

evidence.note: Judd's appeal for support, assistance from earlier British naval contacts, France's reversal and refusal of reparations, and British and American reluctance to pursue the dispute.

segments.summary: British naval contacts helped Judd seek support, but Paris accepted its officers' account and rejected compensation.

segments.title: Similar pretexts accompanied the later American takeover
segments.body: Similar pretexts recur in the later American takeover and the earlier interventions. Britain and France had both been quick to state that they did not want the islands. That reluctance raises a broader historical question about territories imperial powers deliberately avoided acquiring. The closing invitation asks for examples and explanations without answering that question.

evidence.note: Similar pretexts for the later American takeover, British and French reluctance to retain Hawaii, and an unanswered comparative question about imperial expansion.

segments.summary: The later American takeover followed familiar pretexts, while Britain and France had been quick to state that they did not want the islands.
